name: Lunar Prospector

location.name: Shoemaker crater, near the lunar south pole
location.note: NSSDCA gives the impact point as approximately 87.7° S, 42.0° E, in a permanently shadowed crater near the south pole.

headline: It found hints of polar ice, then carried a geologist's ashes into a shadowed crater
story: On 7 January 1998, Lunar Prospector left Cape Canaveral on an Athena 2 rocket. It was a plain drum 1.37 meters wide with three long instrument booms and no onboard computer: every command came from the ground. From a polar orbit about 100 kilometers up, it set out to map what the Moon is made of.

Within two months it had news. In March 1998, NASA announced that its neutron spectrometer had detected hydrogen at both poles, most likely water ice mixed into the soil. NASA called it the first direct evidence of water ice at the lunar poles. The spacecraft also mapped magnetic fields, rock types and the Moon's gravity.

On 31 July 1999, controllers steered it into the shadowed Shoemaker crater near the south pole at about 1.7 kilometers per second, hoping the impact would throw up water vapor that telescopes could see. They saw none. Lunar Prospector carried part of the ashes of the geologist Eugene Shoemaker, and they remain with it in the dark.
